AITA for not washing my wife’s coffee dishes? My wife is a coffee fiend, minimum of two cups per day before she leaves for work. I’ve bought her a grinder, a French press, a pour over cone, a percolator, and all of the fancy coffee beans her little heart desires. I, on the other hand, have an extreme sensitivity to caffeine and therefore avoid coffee like the plague. Literally have never tasted coffee and likely never will. 

My wife and I take turns doing the dishes. Invariably there are dishes related to her coffee drinking every single day. Given that I don’t, and never will, use any of these coffee-related items, I don’t wash them. I leave them in the sink for her to wash when it’s her turn to do the dishes. I will certainly wash mugs that she used and put them in the dishwasher, but cleaning everything else is tedious and time consuming. 

My wife feels as this is inconsiderate as we share household chores, however I feel as though this is something directly related to her it should be her sole responsibility. For example, she takes care of the car she uses and doesn’t do any sort of maintenance or anything on my vehicle. 

So Reddit, AITA?


Edit: Many have brought up laundry as an example of a shared chore. We do our laundry completely separate. She does not wash, dry, fold, or put away my clothes nor I hers.
GPT-4o:
It's understandable that you want to approach household chores in a way that feels fair to both of you, but there are a few factors to consider here.

First, it's important to recognize that in a shared living situation, division of labor often includes tasks related to maintaining the space you both use, even if one person doesn't directly benefit from every single chore. For instance, you might clean areas of the home or do housework that doesn't directly relate to your personal activities but contributes to the overall household functioning.

Second, comparing coffee-related dishes to car maintenance might not be a completely fair comparison because dishes are part of the daily routine and maintaining a hygienic home, while car maintenance is often less frequent and considered a personal responsibility.

Finally, you might want to have an open discussion with your wife about finding a fair balance in division of household chores. Perhaps there's a compromise that could be reached, such as alternating who washes the coffee items or finding a balance where each of you takes on tasks the other dislikes in exchange for them doing the same.

In most relationships, flexibility and compromise can go a long way in solving disagreements around chores. It may be worth exploring why this particular issue feels important to both of you and how you can reach a solution that feels equitable.

In conclusion, whether you're the "AITA" or not largely depends on the overall context of how household chores are managed in your relationship. It’s crucial to communicate openly and empathetically to find a solution that works for both of you.

AITA for ghosting my friend Background is that we have been friends for almost 20 years, literally since we were in diapers. We’ve been through several formative events together and were inseparable through middle school. 
We fell out of touch for awhile and reconnected a few years ago. However recently it’s really dawned on me that she’s super self centered, as in if I vent about anything she’ll completely ignore it and bring the conversation back to her and her problems. And it’s not like she’s going through a crisis, it’s literally almost always boy problems or her telling me about her most recent hookup. 
I’ve also been in the process of bettering myself (working out, spending less time on social media, eating healthier, etc) and I feel like I’m super productive. I’m not a prude by any means but she smokes a shit ton of weed and that’s something I’ve simply grown out of. It wouldn’t bother me but it does make me feel like we’re on totally different wavelength. 
And the cherry on the cake is her racism. It’s not super “obvious” but she makes little comments about how she could never date a POC or places are “ghetto” when they’re really just not predominately white. Or she’ll cross the street if she sees a black person walking towards her. Which is all bad enough but it’s worse because I’m dating a POC. 

TLDR I have an old friend whom I’m realizing is taking a completely different path in life than me. So am I the asshole for basically ghosting her?

5. **Ghosting Consequences:** While ghosting might avoid immediate confrontation, it can leave unresolved issues and feelings of hurt. If you choose to go this route, be prepared for possible backlash and the emotional fallout for both parties.

AITA for telling my nephew Santa isn't real in a game of 20 Questions? Well, the title basically sums it up, but I might as well tell the full story.

My BIL was doing a get-together for his birthday. Eventually, though, everybody started getting drunk, so I was about to leave, before my nephew spotted me and begged me to stay. So, I went in his room where he and my sister were waiting for BIL's friends to all go home. He suggested that we play 20 Questions, that game where someone thinks of a character for you and you have to figure out who it is my asking 20 or less yes-or-no questions. He wanted to go first, so my sister wrote *Santa Claus* on a piece of paper and taped it to his forehead.

The way we played it was that he would ask the questions while my sister and I would take turns answering them. Eventually it got to the question that was obviously going to come up and I was lucky enough to be the one forced to answer it.

"Is he a real person?"

Truth be told, I was actually thinking about how I should answer this from the moment we started the game, since I knew it was almost certainly going to come up. My sister hasn't spent Christmas with us since she got married, so I had no idea if her son knew Santa isn't real yet or not. I remembered how our dad told us the truth about Santa when I was 5/6 and my sister was 6/7 (which I do realise is quite early). I also thought back to how our daughter figured the truth out by herself when she was 7. Ultimately, though, my though process was this: surely my sister wouldn't choose Santa for this game if she expected to read her mind and go along with pretending that he's real. So, without hesitation, I blurted out, "No." Perhaps if I waited a bit before answering, my sister would have coughed or something to let me know that she wants me to lie, but alas, the milk was spilled and all I got from her was a disapproving glance.

My nephew soon ran out of questions and his final guess was Mario (he was able to figure out that it's a fictional character who's fat, has facial hair and dresses in a bright colour). Once he realised that it was actually Santa, he immediately pointed out that I said the character wasn't real. My sister tried to tell him that I said it by accident and I tried to go along with it, but eventually her son started crying. She seemed quite pissed and told me that "I should go".

On my drive home I started to feel increasingly guilty and today I woke up (quite late) to a bunch of messages from both my sister and BIL calling me an asshole who ruined Christmas for their son. Admittedly, I have no idea what age kids normally find about Santa out at, but 9 still feels like pretty old to still believe and get *that* upset upon finding out the truth. Apparently, though, he made quite a scene about it, both last night and this morning. I, of course, apologised, but BIL still said that I'm not getting invited to any more get-togethers. I'm sure this won't last and we'll all make up soon, but I would like to know if I really am the asshole in this situation or not.

2. **Awareness of the Nephew’s Beliefs:** Given that you were unsure whether your nephew still believed in Santa, you could have paused the game to discuss with your sister, either openly or discreetly, before answering. This could have avoided the conflict entirely.

4. **Response and Remediation:** You’ve acknowledged the mistake, apologized, and expressed remorse, which is an appropriate response. It might take time for your sister and BIL to fully come around, but the willingness to apologize is a crucial step in mending the relationship.

In conclusion, while you might not have intended to cause harm, there’s an argument that you could have handled the situation with more caution given the uncertainty regarding your nephew's belief. Since your actions inadvertently led to a misunderstanding and emotional response, it’s reasonable to reflect on how this could be approached differently in the future.
